newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Mediators relieved by peaceful Bosnian poll.
newsitem.headline: Mediators relieved by peaceful Bosnian poll.

text.p: International mediators, relieved by a peaceful vote in Bosnia's first post-war general elections, vowed to press on with nation-building despite Moslem claims of political foul play by Serbs.
They brushed aside a threat by the nationalist Moslem SDA party not to recognise the outcoming of voting in the Bosnian Serb half of the country.

U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke said after a helicopter tour of Bosnia that "what we saw was by and large an election in which we did not see things that would in and of themselves disqualify the electoral process."
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which set up the elections, said the preliminary turnout was 60-70 percent of the 2.9 million electorate.
The OSCE estimated that only 20,000 Moslem refugees ventured into hostile Serb territory to vote in their old homes despite watertight security arrangements by NATO peacekeepers.
Even that figure seemed high, according to reporters who saw only a small numbers of refugees cross the ethnic divide between the Bosnian Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation.

Those who did make the journey appeared to do so in hopes of a simple glimpse of the homes they lost under ethnic cleansing during the war rather than out of any desire to make a political point about Bosnian reintegration.
Voters were electing a three-man Bosnian presidency from each of the Moslem, Serb and Croat communities and national and regional representatives under a plan for the country's reunification.
Moslem leaders late on Saturday threatened to upset the election process by rejecting the Bosnian Serb vote including the election of the Serb candidate to the collective presidency.
Their announcement followed a pledge by Serb hardliners to participate in the presidency despite having campaigned on a separatist platform.
Western officials dismissed the Moslem manoeuvre and Carl Bildt, the chief international civilian representative in Bosnia, told reporters in Sarajevo:

"We were prepared for the worst but we had a day that could be described as dull. We were dreaming of a dull day... we had a few reports of incidents, all of which were dealt with swiftly ...it has been a good, good, good beginning."
Western officials said all parties to the elections knew that conditions would not be fully fair.
Holbrooke dismissed the Moslem challenge as vague and planned to have talks with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Sunday on post-election moves to secure further progress.
The results of the elections, expected to confirm the dominance of the three nationalist parties that led Bosnia into war, are not expected for several days. REUTER
